extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematically-literate readers, and correspondents debating the quadrature (rectification) of the circle
extracted.subtask_description: A historical correspondence arguing whether the circumference and diameter of a circle can be expressed as a finite commensurable ratio (claims P=3.125 vs the established value ~3.14159). Contains proposed proofs, counterarguments, geometric constructions, numerical checks, and appeals to measurement and trigonometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusion of linear and square units
rubrics_metrics.description: This objection referred only to your printed pamphlet ... to avoid the stumbling block, suggested that we should confine the argument solely to the question of ratio of diameter to circumference ... inasmuch as that linear units, and these alone, are the subject of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing diameter vs circumference restrict comparisons to linear measures; do not mix area (square units) with length (linear units) in the same argument unless the unit-conversion is explicitly and correctly handled, because mixing them can produce misleading or invalid deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate existence of a circle with the claimed exact measures
rubrics_metrics.description: What I want you to shew, is, that there can be a circle whose diameter is 1, and whose circumference is, 3.125 accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that a circle has exact finite commensurable measures must be supported either by a constructive mathematical proof showing such a circle exists or by an exact geometrical construction; mere numerical approximations or examples are insufficient to establish exact commensurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measurement as admissible evidence (but with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: By placing stakes on a flat field, and then straining a line from stake to stake, it is easy to obtain a far more convincing result, than any argument will ever produce upon your mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical measurement (measuring tape, stakes, string, carriage wheel) can provide strong practical evidence for or against a proposed finite ratio, but beware the geometric fact that such measurements approximate polygons outside/around the true circle (inscribed vs circumscribed), so their interpretation must consider whether the measured figure corresponds to the exact mathematical object under discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established trigonometric reasoning/proofs to test impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Every school boy of 16 who has been at a Mathematical Academy, knows how to find 'Circular measure,' and cannot know this much without also knowing and seeing why it is impossible the circular circumference should be commensurable with its diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals to standard trigonometric or analytic proofs (those demonstrating incommensurability/irrationality of π or equivalent facts) are legitimate means to refute claims that circumference and diameter are commensurable; such arguments should be used when available and explained clearly to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain internal consistency of definitions and units (role of P)
rubrics_metrics.description: I maintain that if P represents the number of times the diameter of a circle is contained in the circumference, the true circular measure of an angle is dependant on the true value of P being known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions (for example P such that C = P·D) determine derived quantities like circular measure of angles; one must use a single, consistent definition of P and carry it through computations, otherwise compensating errors or apparent agreements may mislead. Tests of hypotheses should check consistency of all derived quantities under the chosen definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygonal (inscribed/circumscribed) approximations converge to circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribe a hexagon in a circle ... as you increase the number of sides ... you will find the perimeter of your polygon approaching nearer and nearer to 3.14159 ... The more sides you take the more decimals you get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximating a circle by regular inscribed or circumscribed polygons is a standard method: increasing the polygon's number of sides yields closer approximations to the true circumference. This method provides convergent numerical evidence for the established value of P but does not by itself yield a finite-exact expression unless accompanied by a limiting argument or exact proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base deductions on arbitrary assumptions that vitiate results
rubrics_metrics.description: In every one of your instances you practically assume a ratio which cannot exist, an assumption which vitiates all your subsequent deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments must not start from an unproved assumption (e.g., assuming a finite rational value for P) and then derive consequences as if established; foundational hypotheses need independent justification, or the conclusions are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic identities among diameter, circumference, and area as consistency checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A represent the area of a circle, C the circumference, D the diameter, and P the number of times the diameter is contained in the circumference, so that C = P x D. Then A = C·D/4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard relations (C = P·D, A = C·D/4, etc.) can be used to test candidate values of P: plug candidate P into these algebraic identities and examine whether resulting quantities have the claimed finiteness, divisibility properties, or decimal behavior across sample diameters to detect contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ explicit numerical examples to test proposed P-values
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: take D=1, D=9, D=4, D=1.28 and compute C, A, and quotients to see whether numerical relations (e.g., quotients being in ratio 1:4 or dividing without remainder) hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through concrete numeric cases to reveal whether hypothesized finite values produce consistent, scale-invariant properties (e.g., exact integer quotients, repeating/non-terminating decimals). Such numerical tests can expose small contradictions or the necessity of infinite decimals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric constructions (rolling wheel / cycloid) to relate linear and produced lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagram: wheel rolling from A to B; the cycloidal arc A C B equals 4 diameters; the plane A B along which the wheel has rolled is exactly equal to the circumference of the wheel. The produced lines have ratios to the diameter expressible in finite terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric constructions involving motion (e.g., rolling circle generating cycloid arcs) can be invoked to relate produced straight/curved lines to the circle's diameter and circumference; such constructions serve as conceptual checks on claims about finite relations between various produced lines and generating lines and can reveal paradoxes if inconsistent assumptions are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer demonstrations intrinsic to the circle rather than only by comparison to other figures
rubrics_metrics.description: I have studiously confined the illustrations of my theory to those relations of a circle which are inherent in its very nature, all the facts and demonstrations brought under your notice being entirely independent of the comparison of a circle with any other geometrical figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, give proofs based on properties inherent to the circle itself rather than relying solely on relations to other figures (squares, polygons), because comparisons may mask assumptions about commensurability or introduce interpretive ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When disputing authorities, explicitly address the accepted proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: I have in my own way examined the various proofs given on this point, and they are neither obvious nor evident to me, and I think I can demonstrate why they are not so, when the proper time for doing so arrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming that established proofs are incorrect or not applicable, explicitly state the points of failure or the step(s) you claim are invalid. Merely asserting authorities are wrong is inadequate; produce a clear refutation of the accepted arguments or demonstrate the flaw.
